title: Ethanol Antisolvent Crystallization of Copper Sulfate Pentahydrate from Acidic Seawater-Based Electrolytes: Solid–Liquid Equilibrium, a Mixed-Solvent Model and the Antisolvent Recovery Balance
content: Antisolvent crystallization with alcohols is under study for rare-earth and other metal sulfates, whereas for copper sulfate the literature offers a purification study and ternary solubilities measured without acid or seawater. We build a single Gibbs-energy function for \(H^+\), \(Na^+\), \(K^+\), \(Mg^{2+}\), \(Cu^{2+}\), \(Cl^-\), \(SO_4^{2-}\) and \(HSO_4^-\) in water + ethanol that reduces to a published Pitzer model when ethanol is absent, with every chemical potential obtained by complex-step differentiation. Four salt coefficients fitted to 33 published solubilities at 298.15 K reproduce \(CuSO_4\), \(Na_2SO_4\), \(K_2SO_4\) and KCl within 2.8, 2.6, 1.8 and 2.3 %, and the data reject a Debye–Hückel and Born treatment based on the bulk permittivity of the mixture. Acid attenuates the antisolvent effect: at an ethanol mass fraction of 0.20 the solubility falls to 0.106 of its ethanol-free value in water and to 0.61 (5–95%: 0.50–0.73) in seawater with 10 wt % \(H_2SO_4\). A decomposition of the response shows that 75 % of this attenuation comes from the stiffness of the solid–liquid equilibrium in the acid electrolyte and the remainder from the shift of the bisulfate equilibrium. For seawater with 1 wt % acid the predicted yield at an antisolvent ratio of 0.25 is 83 %, and ethanol recovery costs 2.5 to 3.2 GJ per tonne of crystal depending on heat recovery, against 6.1 GJ and 2.5 \(m^3\) of evaporated water per tonne for single-effect evaporation. A stability analysis of the same Gibbs function, compared with the measured liquid–liquid binodal of ethanol + \(ZnSO_4\) + water, limits a single-stage dose to a ratio of 0.20. All predictions for acid electrolytes are numerical and await measurement; five experiments that would refute them are specified.
